Medial femoral intermuscular septum.r.description:
MEDIAL FEMORAL INTERMUSCULAR SEPTUM

The medial femoral intermuscular septum (medial intermuscular septum of thigh) is a fibrous partition of the deep fascia (fascia lata) of the thigh, attached along the linea aspera of the femur.

== Location ==

It separates the vastus medialis of the anterior compartment from the adductor muscles and pectineus of the medial compartment of the thigh.

== Function ==

It provides partial origin for the muscles on either side and compartmentalizes the thigh musculature, helping to contain and direct the forces generated during muscle contraction.

Lateral femoral intermuscular septum.r.description:
LATERAL FEMORAL INTERMUSCULAR SEPTUM

The lateral femoral intermuscular septum (lateral intermuscular septum of thigh) is the stronger of the two femoral intermuscular septa, a fibrous partition of the deep fascia (fascia lata) attached along the linea aspera of the femur, extending from the insertion of gluteus maximus to the lateral femoral condyle.

== Location ==

It separates the vastus lateralis of the anterior compartment from the short head of biceps femoris of the posterior compartment of the thigh.

== Function ==

It gives partial origin to both muscles and helps compartmentalize the thigh, and it also receives contributions from the iliotibial tract superficially.

Popliteal fascia.r.description:
POPlITEAL FASCIA


The popliteal fascia covers the popliteal fossa, continuous with fascia lata superiorly and crural fascia inferiorly.

Crural fascia.r.description:
CRURAL FASCIA/
DEEP FASCIA OF LEG


The deep fascia of leg, or crural fascia forms a complete investment to the muscles, and is fused with the periosteum over the subcutaneous surfaces of the bones.

The deep fascia of the leg is continuous above with the fascia lata (deep fascia of the thigh), and is attached around the knee to the patella, the patellar ligament, the tuberosity and condyles of the tibia, and the head of the fibula.

Behind, it forms the popliteal fascia, covering in the popliteal fossa; here it is strengthened by transverse fibers, and perforated by the small saphenous vein.

It receives an expansion from the tendon of the biceps femoris laterally, and from the tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus medially; in front, it blends with the periosteum covering the subcutaneous surface of the tibia, and with that covering the head and malleolus of the fibula; below, it is continuous with the transverse crural and laciniate ligaments.

It is thick and dense in the upper and anterior part of the leg, and gives attachment, by its deep surface, to the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus; but thinner behind, where it covers the gastrocnemius and soleus.

It gives off from its deep surface, on the lateral side of the leg, two strong intermuscular septa, the anterior and posterior peroneal septa, which enclose the peroneus longus and brevis muscles and separate them from the muscles of the anterior and posterior crural regions, and several more slender processes which enclose the individual muscles in each region.

A broad transverse intermuscular septum, called the deep transverse fascia of the leg, intervenes between the superficial and deep posterior crural muscles.

Anterior intermuscular septum of leg.r.description:
ANTERIOR INTERMUSCULAR SEPTUM OF LEG


The anterior intermuscular septum of leg or anterior crural intermuscular septum is a band of fascia which separates the lateral from the anterior compartment of leg.
The deep fascia of leg gives off from its deep surface, on the lateral side of the leg, two strong intermuscular septa, the anterior and posterior peroneal septa, which enclose the peroneus longus and brevis, and separate them from the muscles of the anterior and posterior crural regions, and several more slender processes which enclose the individual muscles in each region.

The posterior intermuscular septum of leg, or posterior crural intermuscular septum is a band of fascia which separates the lateral compartment of leg.
The deep fascia of leg gives off from its deep surface, on the lateral side of the leg, two strong intermuscular septa, the anterior and posterior peroneal septa, which enclose the Peronæi longus and brevis, and separate them from the muscles of the anterior and posterior crural regions, and several more slender processes which enclose the individual muscles in each region.

Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.r.displayName: Right Transverse intermuscular septum of leg
Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.r.description:
TRANSVERSE INTERMUSCULAR SEPTUM OF LEG


The deep transverse fascia or transverse intermuscular septum of leg is a transversely placed, intermuscular septum, from the deep fascia, between the superficial and deep muscles of the back of the leg.

At the sides it is connected to the margins of the tibia and fibula.

Above, where it covers the popliteus, it is thick and dense, and receives an expansion from the tendon of the semimembranosus. 

It is thinner in the middle of the leg; but below, where it covers the tendons passing behind the malleoli, it is thickened and continuous with the laciniate ligament.

Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle.r.displayName: Right Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle
Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle.r.description:
SUPERIOR EXTENSOR RETINACULUM OF ANKLE


The superior extensor retinaculum of the foot (transverse crural ligament) is the upper part of the extensor retinaculum of foot which extends from the ankle to the heelbone.

The superior extensor retinaculum binds down the tendons of extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, peroneus tertius, and tibialis anterior as they descend on the front of the tibia and fibula; under it are found also the anterior tibial vessels and deep peroneal nerve.

It is found on the lateral side of the lower leg, attached laterally to the lower end of the fibula, and medially to the tibia; above it is continuous with the fascia of the leg.

Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle.r.displayName: Right Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle
Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle.r.description:
INFERIOR EXTENSOR RETINACULUM OF ANKLE


The inferior extensor retinaculum of the foot (cruciate crural ligament, lower part of anterior annular ligament) is a Y-shaped band placed in front of the ankle-joint, the stem of the Y being attached laterally to the upper surface of the calcaneus, in front of the depression for the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament; it is directed medialward as a double layer, one lamina passing in front of, and the other behind, the tendons of the peroneus tertius and extensor digitorum longus.

At the medial border of the latter tendon, these two layers join, forming a compartment in which the tendons are enclosed.

From the medial extremity of this sheath, the two limbs of the Y diverge: one is directed upward and medialward, to be attached to the tibial malleolus, passing over the extensor hallucis longus and the vessels and nerves but enclosing the tibialis anterior by a splitting of its fibers.

The other limb extends downward and medialward, to be attached to the border of the plantar aponeurosis, and passes over the tendons of the extensor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior and also the vessels and nerves.

Superior fibular retinaculum.r.description:
SUPERIOR FIBULAR RETINACULUM


Superior ligament for the fibular muscles going from the lateral malleolus to the calcaneus.

Inferior fibular retinaculum.r.description:
INFERIOR FIBULAR RETINACULUM


Inferior ligament for the fibularis longus muscle and fibularis brevis muscle, going from the inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle to the lateral surface of calcaneus.

A bundle of fibers goes to the fibular trochlea and separates the fibularis brevis muscle from the fibularis longus muscle.

Strengthening ligament of the dorsal fascia of foot.

Superficial transverse metatarsal ligame.description:
SUPERFICIAL TRANSVERSE METATARSAL LIGAMENT


The transverse metatarsal ligament is a narrow band which runs across and connects together the heads of all the metatarsal bones. 

It is blended anteriorly with the plantar (glenoid) ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal articulations.

Its plantar surface is concave where the Flexor tendons run below it. 

Above it, the tendons of the Interossei pass to their insertions.

Its homologue in the hand is the transverse metacarpal ligament, which connects the metacarpals to each other.

Plantar aponeurosis.r.description:
PLANTAR APONEUROSIS


The plantar fascia is the thick connective tissue (aponeurosis) which supports the arch on the bottom (plantar side) of the foot. 

It runs from the tuberosity of the calcaneus (heel bone) forward to the heads of the metatarsal bones (the bone between each toe and the bones of the mid-foot). 


The plantar fascia is a broad structure that spans between the medial calcaneal tubercle and the proximal phalanges of the toes. 

Recent studies suggest that the plantar fascia is actually an aponeurosis rather than true fascia. 

The Dorland’s Medical Dictionary defines an aponeurosis as: (i) a white, flattened or ribbon-like tendinous expansion, serving mainly to connect a muscle with the parts that it moves, (ii) a term formerly applied to certain fasciae. 

Further, it defines the plantar aponeurosis as bands of fibrous connective tissue radiating toward the bases of the toes from the medial process of the tuber calcanei (posterior half of the calcaneus).

The plantar fascia is made up of predominantly longitudinally oriented collagen fibers. 

There are three distinct structural components: the medial component, the central component (plantar aponeurosis), and the lateral component (see diagram at right). 

The central component is the largest and most prominent.

In younger people the plantar fascia is also intimately related to the Achilles tendon, with a continuous fascial connection between the two from the distal aspect of the Achilles to the origin of the plantar fascia at the calcaneal tubercle. 

However, the continuity of this connection decreases with age to a point that in the elderly there are few, if any, connecting fibers. 

There are also distinct attachments of the plantar fascia and the Achilles tendon to the calcaneus so the two do not directly contact each other. 

Nevertheless, there is an indirect relationship whereby if the toes are dorsiflexed, the plantar fascia tightens via the windlass mechanism. 

If a tensile force is then generated in the Achilles tendon it will increase tensile strain in the plantar fascia. 

Clinically, this relationship has been used as a basis for treatment for plantar fasciitis, with stretches and night stretch splinting being applied to the gastrocnemius/soleus muscle unit.


==Function==

The effect of dorsiflexing the toes on arch height (A). The windlass mechanism (B).

The plantar fascia contributes to support of arch of the foot by acting as a tie-rod, where it undergoes tension when the foot bears weight. One biomechanical model estimated it carries as much as 14% of the total load of the foot. 

In an experiment using cadavers, it was found that failure of the plantar fascia averaged at loads of 1189 ± 244 newtons (121 ± 24 kgf or 267 ± 55 lbf). 

Failure most often occurred at the proximal attachment to the calcaneus, which is consistent with the usual location of symptoms (i.e. in plantar fasciitis). 

Complete rupture or surgical release of the plantar fascia leads to a decrease in arch stiffness and a significant collapse of the longitudinal arch of the foot. 

By modeling it was predicted such conditions would result in a 17% increase in vertical displacement and a 15% increase in horizontal elongation of the foot when it was loaded at 683 newtons (154 lbf).

Surgical release also significantly increases both stress in the plantar ligaments and plantar pressures under the metatarsal heads. 

Although most of the figures mentioned above are from either cadaver studies or investigations using models, they highlight the relatively large load the plantar fascia is subjected to while contributing to the structural integrity of the foot.


==Gait==

The plantar fascia also has an important role in dynamic function during gait. 

It was found the plantar fascia continuously elongated during the contact phase of gait.

It went through rapid elongation before and immediately after mid-stance, reaching a maximum of 9% to 12% elongation between mid-stance and toe-off.

During this phase the plantar fascia behaves like a spring, which may assist in conserving energy. 

In addition, the plantar fascia has a critical role in normal mechanical function of the foot, contributing to the "windlass mechanism". 

When the toes are dorsiflexed in the propulsive phase of gait, the plantar fascia becomes tense, resulting in elevation of the longitudinal arch and shortening of the foot. 

One can liken this mechanism to a cable being wound around the drum of a windlass (see 3B); the plantar fascia being the cable, the metatarsal head the drum, and the handle, the proximal phalanx.

Flexor retinaculum of ankle.r.description:
FLEXOR RETINACULUM OF ANKLE


The flexor retinaculum of foot (laciniate ligament, internal annular ligament) is a strong fibrous band in the foot.


== Structure ==

The flexor retinaculum of the foot extends from the medial malleolus above, to the calcaneus below. 

This converts a series of bony grooves into canals for the passage of the tendons of the flexor muscles and the posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve into the sole of the foot, known as the tarsal tunnel.

It is continuous by its upper border with the deep fascia of the leg, and by its lower border with the plantar aponeurosis and the fibers of origin of the abductor hallucis muscle.

Enumerated from the medial side, the four canals which it forms transmit the tendons of the tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus muscles; the posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve, which run through a broad space beneath the ligament; and lastly, in a canal formed partly by the talus, the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus.


== Clinical significance ==

Tarsal tunnel syndrome can be caused by entrapment of the tibial nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum of the foot. 

This is characterized by pain, numbness, and tingling of the medial plantar surface of the foot. 

This is made worse by standing and walking, and often worse at night. 

Tinel's sign can be elicited by tapping the part of the flexor retinaculum of the foot over the tibial nerve.

Iliopectineal arch.r.description:
ILIOPECTINEAL ARCH

The iliopectineal arch is a thickened band of fused iliac and psoas fascia that lies deep to the inguinal ligament, passing from the posterior surface of the inguinal ligament anteriorly, across the front of the femoral nerve, to attach posteriorly to the iliopubic (iliopectineal) eminence of the hip bone.

== Function ==

It subdivides the space deep to the inguinal ligament into a lateral muscular lacuna, which transmits the iliopsoas muscle and femoral nerve, and a medial vascular lacuna, which contains the femoral artery, vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes within the femoral sheath.

== Relations ==

When a psoas minor muscle is present, its tendon blends with the iliopectineal arch; the arch is also continuous with the thoracolumbar fascia posteriorly.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is occasionally surgically divided in the treatment of femoral nerve entrapment beneath the inguinal ligament.

The deep fascia of leg, or crural fascia forms a complete investment to the muscles, and is fused with the periosteum over the subcutaneous surfaces of the bones.

The deep fascia of the leg is continuous above with the fascia lata (deep fascia of the thigh), and is attached around the knee to the patella, the patellar ligament, the tuberosity and condyles of the tibia, and the head of the fibula.

Behind, it forms the popliteal fascia, covering in the popliteal fossa; here it is strengthened by transverse fibers, and perforated by the small saphenous vein.

It receives an expansion from the tendon of the biceps femoris laterally, and from the tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus medially; in front, it blends with the periosteum covering the subcutaneous surface of the tibia, and with that covering the head and malleolus of the fibula; below, it is continuous with the transverse crural and laciniate ligaments.

It is thick and dense in the upper and anterior part of the leg, and gives attachment, by its deep surface, to the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus; but thinner behind, where it covers the gastrocnemius and soleus.

It gives off from its deep surface, on the lateral side of the leg, two strong intermuscular septa, the anterior and posterior peroneal septa, which enclose the peroneus longus and brevis muscles and separate them from the muscles of the anterior and posterior crural regions, and several more slender processes which enclose the individual muscles in each region.

A broad transverse intermuscular septum, called the deep transverse fascia of the leg, intervenes between the superficial and deep posterior crural muscles.

Anterior intermuscular septum of leg.l.displayName: Left Anterior intermuscular septum of leg
Anterior intermuscular septum of leg.l.description:
ANTERIOR INTERMUSCULAR SEPTUM OF LEG


The anterior intermuscular septum of leg or anterior crural intermuscular septum is a band of fascia which separates the lateral from the anterior compartment of leg.
The deep fascia of leg gives off from its deep surface, on the lateral side of the leg, two strong intermuscular septa, the anterior and posterior peroneal septa, which enclose the peroneus longus and brevis, and separate them from the muscles of the anterior and posterior crural regions, and several more slender processes which enclose the individual muscles in each region.

Posterior intermuscular septum of leg.l.displayName: Left Posterior intermuscular septum of leg
Posterior intermuscular septum of leg.l.description:

The posterior intermuscular septum of leg, or posterior crural intermuscular septum is a band of fascia which separates the lateral compartment of leg.
The deep fascia of leg gives off from its deep surface, on the lateral side of the leg, two strong intermuscular septa, the anterior and posterior peroneal septa, which enclose the Peronæi longus and brevis, and separate them from the muscles of the anterior and posterior crural regions, and several more slender processes which enclose the individual muscles in each region.

Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.l.displayName: Left Transverse intermuscular septum of leg
Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.l.description:
TRANSVERSE INTERMUSCULAR SEPTUM OF LEG


The deep transverse fascia or transverse intermuscular septum of leg is a transversely placed, intermuscular septum, from the deep fascia, between the superficial and deep muscles of the back of the leg.

At the sides it is connected to the margins of the tibia and fibula.

Above, where it covers the popliteus, it is thick and dense, and receives an expansion from the tendon of the semimembranosus. 

It is thinner in the middle of the leg; but below, where it covers the tendons passing behind the malleoli, it is thickened and continuous with the laciniate ligament.

Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle.l.displayName: Left Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle
Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle.l.description:
SUPERIOR EXTENSOR RETINACULUM OF ANKLE


The superior extensor retinaculum of the foot (transverse crural ligament) is the upper part of the extensor retinaculum of foot which extends from the ankle to the heelbone.

The superior extensor retinaculum binds down the tendons of extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, peroneus tertius, and tibialis anterior as they descend on the front of the tibia and fibula; under it are found also the anterior tibial vessels and deep peroneal nerve.

It is found on the lateral side of the lower leg, attached laterally to the lower end of the fibula, and medially to the tibia; above it is continuous with the fascia of the leg. 



https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_extensor_retinaculum_of_foot

Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle.l.displayName: Left Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle
Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle.l.description:
INFERIOR EXTENSOR RETINACULUM OF ANKLE


The inferior extensor retinaculum of the foot (cruciate crural ligament, lower part of anterior annular ligament) is a Y-shaped band placed in front of the ankle-joint, the stem of the Y being attached laterally to the upper surface of the calcaneus, in front of the depression for the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament; it is directed medialward as a double layer, one lamina passing in front of, and the other behind, the tendons of the peroneus tertius and extensor digitorum longus.

At the medial border of the latter tendon, these two layers join, forming a compartment in which the tendons are enclosed.

From the medial extremity of this sheath, the two limbs of the Y diverge: one is directed upward and medialward, to be attached to the tibial malleolus, passing over the extensor hallucis longus and the vessels and nerves but enclosing the tibialis anterior by a splitting of its fibers.

The other limb extends downward and medialward, to be attached to the border of the plantar aponeurosis, and passes over the tendons of the extensor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior and also the vessels and nerves.

Superior fibular retinaculum.l.description:
SUPERIOR FIBULAR RETINACULUM


Superior ligament for the fibular muscles going from the lateral malleolus to the calcaneus.

Inferior fibular retinaculum.l.description:
INFERIOR FIBULAR RETINACULUM


Inferior ligament for the fibularis longus muscle and fibularis brevis muscle, going from the inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle to the lateral surface of calcaneus.

A bundle of fibers goes to the fibular trochlea and separates the fibularis brevis muscle from the fibularis longus muscle.

Strengthening ligament of the dorsal fascia of foot.

Superficial transverse metatarsal ligame.description:
SUPERFICIAL TRANSVERSE METATARSAL LIGAMENT


The transverse metatarsal ligament is a narrow band which runs across and connects together the heads of all the metatarsal bones. 

It is blended anteriorly with the plantar (glenoid) ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal articulations.

Its plantar surface is concave where the Flexor tendons run below it. 

Above it, the tendons of the Interossei pass to their insertions.

Its homologue in the hand is the transverse metacarpal ligament, which connects the metacarpals to each other.

Plantar aponeurosis.l.description:
PLANTAR APONEUROSIS


The plantar fascia is the thick connective tissue (aponeurosis) which supports the arch on the bottom (plantar side) of the foot. 

It runs from the tuberosity of the calcaneus (heel bone) forward to the heads of the metatarsal bones (the bone between each toe and the bones of the mid-foot). 


The plantar fascia is a broad structure that spans between the medial calcaneal tubercle and the proximal phalanges of the toes. 

Recent studies suggest that the plantar fascia is actually an aponeurosis rather than true fascia. 

The Dorland’s Medical Dictionary defines an aponeurosis as: (i) a white, flattened or ribbon-like tendinous expansion, serving mainly to connect a muscle with the parts that it moves, (ii) a term formerly applied to certain fasciae. 

Further, it defines the plantar aponeurosis as bands of fibrous connective tissue radiating toward the bases of the toes from the medial process of the tuber calcanei (posterior half of the calcaneus).

The plantar fascia is made up of predominantly longitudinally oriented collagen fibers. 

There are three distinct structural components: the medial component, the central component (plantar aponeurosis), and the lateral component (see diagram at right). 

The central component is the largest and most prominent.

In younger people the plantar fascia is also intimately related to the Achilles tendon, with a continuous fascial connection between the two from the distal aspect of the Achilles to the origin of the plantar fascia at the calcaneal tubercle. 

However, the continuity of this connection decreases with age to a point that in the elderly there are few, if any, connecting fibers. 

There are also distinct attachments of the plantar fascia and the Achilles tendon to the calcaneus so the two do not directly contact each other. 

Nevertheless, there is an indirect relationship whereby if the toes are dorsiflexed, the plantar fascia tightens via the windlass mechanism. 

If a tensile force is then generated in the Achilles tendon it will increase tensile strain in the plantar fascia. 

Clinically, this relationship has been used as a basis for treatment for plantar fasciitis, with stretches and night stretch splinting being applied to the gastrocnemius/soleus muscle unit.


==Function==

The effect of dorsiflexing the toes on arch height (A). The windlass mechanism (B).

The plantar fascia contributes to support of arch of the foot by acting as a tie-rod, where it undergoes tension when the foot bears weight. One biomechanical model estimated it carries as much as 14% of the total load of the foot. 

In an experiment using cadavers, it was found that failure of the plantar fascia averaged at loads of 1189 ± 244 newtons (121 ± 24 kgf or 267 ± 55 lbf). 

Failure most often occurred at the proximal attachment to the calcaneus, which is consistent with the usual location of symptoms (i.e. in plantar fasciitis). 

Complete rupture or surgical release of the plantar fascia leads to a decrease in arch stiffness and a significant collapse of the longitudinal arch of the foot. 

By modeling it was predicted such conditions would result in a 17% increase in vertical displacement and a 15% increase in horizontal elongation of the foot when it was loaded at 683 newtons (154 lbf).

Surgical release also significantly increases both stress in the plantar ligaments and plantar pressures under the metatarsal heads. 

Although most of the figures mentioned above are from either cadaver studies or investigations using models, they highlight the relatively large load the plantar fascia is subjected to while contributing to the structural integrity of the foot.


==Gait==

The plantar fascia also has an important role in dynamic function during gait. 

It was found the plantar fascia continuously elongated during the contact phase of gait.

It went through rapid elongation before and immediately after mid-stance, reaching a maximum of 9% to 12% elongation between mid-stance and toe-off.

During this phase the plantar fascia behaves like a spring, which may assist in conserving energy. 

In addition, the plantar fascia has a critical role in normal mechanical function of the foot, contributing to the "windlass mechanism". 

When the toes are dorsiflexed in the propulsive phase of gait, the plantar fascia becomes tense, resulting in elevation of the longitudinal arch and shortening of the foot. 

One can liken this mechanism to a cable being wound around the drum of a windlass (see 3B); the plantar fascia being the cable, the metatarsal head the drum, and the handle, the proximal phalanx.

Flexor retinaculum of ankle.l.description:
FLEXOR RETINACULUM OF ANKLE


The flexor retinaculum of foot (laciniate ligament, internal annular ligament) is a strong fibrous band in the foot.


== Structure ==

The flexor retinaculum of the foot extends from the medial malleolus above, to the calcaneus below. 

This converts a series of bony grooves into canals for the passage of the tendons of the flexor muscles and the posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve into the sole of the foot, known as the tarsal tunnel.

It is continuous by its upper border with the deep fascia of the leg, and by its lower border with the plantar aponeurosis and the fibers of origin of the abductor hallucis muscle.

Enumerated from the medial side, the four canals which it forms transmit the tendons of the tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus muscles; the posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve, which run through a broad space beneath the ligament; and lastly, in a canal formed partly by the talus, the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus.


== Clinical significance ==

Tarsal tunnel syndrome can be caused by entrapment of the tibial nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum of the foot. 

This is characterized by pain, numbness, and tingling of the medial plantar surface of the foot. 

This is made worse by standing and walking, and often worse at night. 

Tinel's sign can be elicited by tapping the part of the flexor retinaculum of the foot over the tibial nerve.



https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexor_retinaculum_of_foot

Iliopectineal arch.l.description:
ILIOPECTINEAL ARCH

The iliopectineal arch is a thickened band of fused iliac and psoas fascia that lies deep to the inguinal ligament, passing from the posterior surface of the inguinal ligament anteriorly, across the front of the femoral nerve, to attach posteriorly to the iliopubic (iliopectineal) eminence of the hip bone.

== Function ==

It subdivides the space deep to the inguinal ligament into a lateral muscular lacuna, which transmits the iliopsoas muscle and femoral nerve, and a medial vascular lacuna, which contains the femoral artery, vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes within the femoral sheath.

== Relations ==

When a psoas minor muscle is present, its tendon blends with the iliopectineal arch; the arch is also continuous with the thoracolumbar fascia posteriorly.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is occasionally surgically divided in the treatment of femoral nerve entrapment beneath the inguinal ligament.

External anal sphincter.r.description:
EXTERNAL ANAL SPHINCTER


The external anal sphincter (or sphincter ani externus ) is a flat plane of skeletal muscle fibers, elliptical in shape and intimately adherent to the skin surrounding the margin of the anus.


== Anatomy ==

The external anal sphincter measures about 8 to 10 cm in length, from its anterior to its posterior extremity, and is about 2.5 cm opposite the anus, the sphincter muscle retracts on defecating.

It consists of two layers: superficial and deep.

The superficial layer, constitutes the main portion of the muscle, and arises from a narrow tendinous band, the anococcygeal raphe, which stretches from the tip of the coccyx to the posterior margin of the anus; it forms two flattened planes of muscular tissue, which encircle the anus and meet in front to be inserted into the central tendinous point of the perineum, joining with the superficial transverse perineal muscle, the levator ani, and the bulbospongiosus muscle also known as the bulbocavernosus.

The deeper layer forms a complete sphincter to the anal canal. 

Its fibers surround the canal, closely applied to the internal anal sphincter, and in front blend with the other muscles at the central point of the perineum.

In a considerable proportion of cases the fibers decussate in front of the anus, and are continuous with the superficial transverse perineal muscle.

Posteriorly, they are not attached to the coccyx, but are continuous with those of the opposite side behind the anal canal.

The upper edge of the muscle is ill-defined, since fibers are given off from it to join the levator ani.


== Actions ==

(1) Like other muscles, it is always in a state of tonic contraction, and having no antagonistic muscle it keeps the anal canal and orifice shut.

(2) It can be put into a condition of greater contraction under the influence of the will, so as more firmly to occlude the anal aperture, in expiratory efforts unconnected with defecation.

(3) Taking its fixed point at the coccyx, it helps to fix the central point of the perineum, so that the bulbospongiosus muscle may act from this fixed point.



https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_anal_sphincter

Clavipectoral fascia.r.description:
CLAVIPECTORAL FASCIA


The clavipectoral fascia (costocoracoid membrane; coracoclavicular fascia) is a strong fascia situated under cover of the clavicular portion of the pectoralis major.

It occupies the interval between the pectoralis minor and subclavius, and protects the axillary vein and artery, and axillary nerve.

Traced upward, it splits to enclose the subclavius, and its two layers are attached to the clavicle, one in front of and the other behind the muscle; the deep layer fuses with the deep cervical fascia and with the sheath of the axillary vessels.

Medially, it blends with the fascia covering the first two intercostal spaces, and is attached also to the first rib medial to the origin of the subclavius.

Laterally, it is very thick and dense, and is attached to the coracoid process.

The portion extending from the first rib to the coracoid process is often whiter and denser than the rest, and is sometimes called the costocoracoid membrane.

Below this it is thin, and at the upper border of the pectoralis minor it splits into two layers to invest the muscle; from the lower border of the pectoralis minor it is continued downward to join the axillary fascia, and lateralward to join the fascia over the short head of the biceps brachii.

The clavipectoral fascia is pierced by the cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery and vein, lymphatics and lateral pectoral nerve.



https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavipectoral_fascia

Iliopsoas fascia.r.description:
ILIOPSOAS FASCIA/
ILIAC FASCIA


The iliac fascia, or Abernethy's fascia, is a fascia in the region of the ilium of the pelvis.

It has the following connections:

-laterally, to the whole length of the inner lip of the iliac crest.
medially, to the linea terminalis of the lesser pelvis, where it is continuous with the periosteum.

-At the iliopectineal eminence it receives the tendon of insertion of the Psoas minor, when that muscle exists.

-Lateral to the femoral vessels it is intimately connected to the posterior margin of the inguinal ligament, and is continuous with the transversalis fascia.

-Immediately lateral to the femoral vessels the iliac fascia is prolonged backward and medialward from the inguinal ligament as a band, the iliopectineal fascia, which is attached to the iliopectineal eminence.

This fascia divides the space between the inguinal ligament and the hip bone into two lacunæ or compartments:

-the medial vascular lacuna transmits the femoral vessels.
-the lateral muscular lacuna transmits the Psoas major and Iliacus and the femoral nerve.Medial to the vessels the iliac fascia is attached to the pectineal line behind the conjoint tendon, where it is again continuous with the transversalis fascia.

Transversalis fascia.description:
TRANSVERSALIS FASCIA


The transversalis fascia (or transverse fascia) is a thin aponeurotic membrane which lies between the inner surface of the transverse abdominal muscle and the parietal peritoneum.

It forms part of the general layer of fascia lining the abdominal parietes, and is directly continuous with the iliac fascia, internal spermatic, and pelvic fasciae.

In the inguinal region, the transversalis fascia is thick and dense in structure and is joined by fibers from the aponeurosis of the transverse abdominal. 

It becomes thin as it ascends to the diaphragm and blends with the fascia covering the under surface of this muscle.


== Borders ==

Behind, it is lost in the fat which covers the posterior surfaces of the kidneys.

Below, it has the following attachments: posteriorly, to the whole length of the iliac crest, between the attachments of the transverse abdominal and Iliacus; between the anterior superior iliac spine and the femoral vessels it is connected to the posterior margin of the inguinal ligament, and is there continuous with the iliac fascia.

Medial to the femoral vessels it is thin and attached to the pubis and pectineal line, behind the inguinal falx, with which it is united; it descends in front of the femoral vessels to form the anterior wall of the femoral sheath.

Beneath the inguinal ligament it is strengthened by a band of fibrous tissue, which is only loosely connected to the ligament, and is specialized as the iliopubic tract.


== Opening ==

The spermatic cord in the male and the round ligament of the uterus in the female pass through the transverse fascia at the deep inguinal ring the entrance to the inguinal canal. 

This opening is not visible externally. 

In the male the transverse fascia extends downwards as the internal spermatic fascia.

Subtendinous bursa of trapezius muscle.r.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of trapezius muscle
Subtendinous bursa of trapezius muscle.r.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF TRAPEZIUS MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of trapezius muscle (also called the scapulotrapezial bursa) is a small synovial-lined sac located between the deep surface of the tendinous attachment of the trapezius muscle and the superomedial angle of the scapula, near the root of the scapular spine.

== Function ==

Its role is to reduce friction between the trapezius tendon and the underlying bony surface of the scapula during scapular elevation, retraction, and rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

Repetitive shoulder-shrugging movements or direct trauma can irritate this bursa, producing localized pain over the superomedial scapular border that is aggravated by trapezius contraction.

Subcutaneous acromial bursa.r.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS ACROMIAL BURSA

The subcutaneous acromial bursa is a small synovial bursa situated between the skin and the superficial surface of the acromion process of the scapula.

== Function ==

It cushions and reduces friction between the skin and the underlying bony acromion during shoulder movement and when pressure is applied directly over the point of the shoulder.

== Clinical relevance ==

Being subcutaneous, it can become inflamed following direct trauma or prolonged pressure over the shoulder, producing a tender, sometimes visibly swollen area over the acromion.

Subacromial bursa.r.description:
SUBACROMIAL BURSA


The subacromial bursa is the synovial cavity located just below the acromion, which communicates with the subdeltoid bursa in most individuals, forming the so-called subacromial-subdeltoid bursa (SSB).

The SSB bursa is located deep to the deltoid muscle and the coracoacromial arch and extends laterally beyond the humeral attachment of the rotator cuff, anteriorly to overlie the intertubercular groove, medially to the acromioclavicular joint, and posteriorly over the rotator cuff. 

The SSB decreases friction, and allows free motion of the rotator cuff relative to the coracoacromial arch and the deltoid muscle.

Since then, histologic studies have documented that synovial membrane may undergo inflammatory and/or degenerative changes and many now believe that they correspond to different stages in the spectrum of disease, with long-lasting inflammation leading to degeneration and fibrosis.

The subacromial bursa is the synovial cavity located just below the acromion, which communicates with the subdeltoid bursa in most individuals, forming the so-called subacromial-subdeltoid bursa (SSB).

The SSB bursa is located deep to the deltoid muscle and the coracoacromial arch and extends laterally beyond the humeral attachment of the rotator cuff, anteriorly to overlie the intertubercular groove, medially to the acromioclavicular joint, and posteriorly over the rotator cuff. 

The SSB decreases friction, and allows free motion of the rotator cuff relative to the coracoacromial arch and the deltoid muscle.

Since then, histologic studies have documented that synovial membrane may undergo inflammatory and/or degenerative changes and many now believe that they correspond to different stages in the spectrum of disease, with long-lasting inflammation leading to degeneration and fibrosis.

Subdeltoid bursa.r.description:
SUBDELTOID BURSA

The subdeltoid bursa is a large synovial sac located between the deep surface of the deltoid muscle and the underlying joint capsule of the glenohumeral joint and the greater tubercle of the humerus. In most individuals it is continuous with the subacromial bursa, together forming the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa.

== Relations ==

It lies superficial to the supraspinatus tendon and the rotator cuff, extending laterally beyond the humeral insertion of the cuff tendons.

== Function ==

It permits smooth, low-friction gliding of the deltoid muscle and rotator cuff tendons beneath the coracoacromial arch during arm abduction and elevation.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is one of the most frequent sites of shoulder bursitis and is commonly involved in subacromial impingement syndrome and rotator cuff pathology.

Coracobrachial bursa.r.description:
CORACOBRACHIAL BURSA

The coracobrachial bursa is a small synovial bursa located deep to the conjoined tendon of the coracobrachialis muscle and the short head of the biceps brachii, near the tip of the coracoid process of the scapula, and superficial to the subscapularis tendon.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the conjoined tendon and the subscapularis tendon as they glide over one another during shoulder rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

It may communicate with the neighbouring subcoracoid bursa and, less commonly, with the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa; inflammation here can contribute to anterior shoulder pain during internal and external rotation.

Subtendinous bursa of infraspinatus musc.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of infraspinatus muscle
Subtendinous bursa of infraspinatus musc.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF INFRASPINATUS MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of the infraspinatus muscle is a synovial sac situated between the tendon of the infraspinatus muscle and the posterior aspect of the glenohumeral joint capsule, close to its insertion on the greater tubercle of the humerus.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the infraspinatus tendon and the joint capsule during the arc of external rotation of the shoulder.

== Clinical relevance ==

This bursa may become symptomatic in association with posterior rotator cuff tendinopathy or degenerative capsular changes.

Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle
Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle.baseName: Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle
Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF TERES MAJOR MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of the teres major muscle is a small synovial sac found between the tendon of teres major and the tendon of latissimus dorsi as they converge near their common insertion on the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus, or between the teres major tendon and the underlying bone.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between these adjacent tendons during shoulder adduction, extension, and internal rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

Overuse of the shoulder extensors and internal rotators (e.g., in swimming or throwing) can irritate this bursa, producing posterior axillary or medial arm discomfort.

Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii mu.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle
Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii mu.baseName: Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle
Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii mu.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF TRICEPS BRACHII MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of the triceps brachii muscle is a synovial bursa located between the triceps tendon and the olecranon process of the ulna, just proximal to the tendon's insertion.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the gliding triceps tendon and the underlying bone during flexion and extension of the elbow.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is distinct from the more superficial subcutaneous olecranon bursa; inflammation of the subtendinous bursa is less common but can occur with repetitive elbow extension activities and may mimic triceps tendinopathy.

Bicipitoradial bursa.r.description:
BICIPITORADIAL BURSA


The bicipitoradial bursa is a bursa located between the distal tendon of the biceps brachii muscle and the anterior part of the tuberosity of the radius. 

It partially or completely wraps around the biceps tendon. 

It ensures frictionless motion between the biceps tendon and the proximal radius during pronation and supination of the forearm. 

With pronation, the tuberosity of the radius rotates posteriorly, causing compression of the bursa between the biceps tendon and the radial tuberosity.

The bicipitoradial bursa is one of the two bursae in the cubital fossa, the other being the interosseous bursa.

Inflammation of the bicipitoradial bursa or bicipitoradial bursitis is a rare condition and only few reports can be found in literature. 

In severe cases, the bursa is distended by synovial debris and can cause compression of the posterior interosseous nerve.



https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicipitoradial_bursa

Subcutaneous trochanteric bursa.r.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS TROCHANTERIC BURSA

The subcutaneous trochanteric bursa is a small synovial sac located between the skin and the subcutaneous surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.

== Function ==

It cushions and reduces friction between the skin and the bony prominence of the greater trochanter, particularly during side-lying or direct pressure over the hip.

== Clinical relevance ==

It can become inflamed following direct trauma or prolonged pressure, contributing to lateral hip tenderness that must be distinguished from deeper trochanteric bursitis.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius mus.description:
TROCHANTERIC BURSA OF GLUTEUS MEDIUS MUSCLE

The trochanteric bursa of the gluteus medius muscle (subgluteus medius bursa) lies deep to the distal insertion of the gluteus medius tendon, overlying the superior facet of the greater trochanter of the femur.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the gluteus medius tendon and the greater trochanter during hip abduction and rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is one of the bursae implicated in greater trochanteric pain syndrome, often occurring together with gluteus medius tendinopathy.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus mu.displayName: Right Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus mu.baseName: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus mu.description:
TROCHANTERIC BURSA OF GLUTEUS MAXIMUS MUSCLE

The trochanteric bursa of the gluteus maximus muscle (subgluteus maximus/greater trochanteric bursa) is the largest bursa of the hip region, situated between the deep surface of the gluteus maximus muscle and iliotibial tract and the posterolateral surface of the greater trochanter.

== Function ==

It allows the gluteus maximus and the overlying iliotibial tract to glide smoothly over the greater trochanter during hip extension and rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

This bursa is the principal structure involved in classic greater trochanteric bursitis, now more broadly termed greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus mu.description:
TROCHANTERIC BURSA OF GLUTEUS MINIMUS MUSCLE

The trochanteric bursa of the gluteus minimus muscle (subgluteus minimus bursa) lies beneath the tendon of the gluteus minimus muscle, at the anterior facet of the greater trochanter of the femur.

== Function ==

It minimizes friction between the gluteus minimus tendon and the anterior trochanteric facet during hip abduction and internal rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

It can be involved, along with the gluteus medius bursa, in greater trochanteric pain syndrome and gluteus minimus tendinopathy, common causes of chronic lateral hip pain.

Bursa of piriformis muscle.r.description:
BURSA OF PIRIFORMIS MUSCLE

The bursa of the piriformis muscle (piriformis bursa, also described as the posterior subgluteus medius bursa) is a small synovial sac located deep to the piriformis tendon near its insertion on the greater trochanter of the femur.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the piriformis tendon and the adjacent gluteus medius tendon and bony trochanter during hip rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

Inflammation of this bursa can contribute to deep gluteal and lateral hip pain and may overlap clinically with piriformis syndrome.

Sciatic bursa of obturator internus.r.displayName: Right Sciatic bursa of obturator internus
Sciatic bursa of obturator internus.r.description:
SCIATIC BURSA OF OBTURATOR INTERNUS

The sciatic bursa of obturator internus is a synovial bursa located between the tendon of the obturator internus muscle and the ischium, near where the tendon turns sharply around the lesser sciatic notch.

== Function ==

It reduces friction as the obturator internus tendon changes direction over the bony margin of the lesser sciatic notch during hip rotation.

== Clinical relevance ==

This bursa lies close to the sciatic nerve and pudendal neurovascular structures, and its inflammation can contribute to deep buttock pain in the differential diagnosis of sciatica-like symptoms.

Subtendinous bursa of obturator internus.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of obturator internus
Subtendinous bursa of obturator internus.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF OBTURATOR INTERNUS

The subtendinous bursa of obturator internus is a synovial sac situated between the obturator internus tendon and the ischium, deep to the tendon at the level of the hip joint capsule, distinct from the more peripheral sciatic bursa of the same muscle.

== Function ==

It cushions the obturator internus tendon against the underlying bone as the muscle acts to laterally rotate and abduct the flexed hip.

== Clinical relevance ==

Bursal irritation here is an uncommon but recognized cause of deep posterior hip pain.

Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle..baseName: Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle
Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle..description:
SCIATIC BURSA OF GLUTEUS MAXIMUS MUSCLE

The sciatic bursa of the gluteus maximus muscle (ischiogluteal bursa) is located between the lower part of the gluteus maximus muscle and the ischial tuberosity.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the gluteus maximus and the bony ischial tuberosity, particularly during sitting and hip extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

Prolonged sitting on hard surfaces can inflame this bursa, producing 'weaver's bottom' (ischiogluteal bursitis), which presents as pain over the ischial tuberosity, sometimes radiating along the course of the sciatic nerve.

Intermuscular gluteal bursae.r.description:
INTERMUSCULAR GLUTEAL BURSAE

The intermuscular gluteal bursae are a variable number of small synovial bursae found between the overlapping muscle bellies of the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus muscles in the buttock region.

== Function ==

They facilitate smooth gliding between adjacent gluteal muscle layers as these muscles contract independently during hip movement.

== Clinical relevance ==

These bursae are inconsistently present and rarely a primary source of pathology, but they can be involved secondarily in extensive greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

(Iliopectineal bursa).r.description:
ILIOPECTINEAL BURSA

The iliopectineal bursa (iliopsoas bursa) is the largest bursa in the human body, situated deep to the musculotendinous portion of the iliopsoas muscle, anterior to the hip joint capsule, bordered medially by the pectineus muscle and laterally by the anterior inferior iliac spine.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the iliopsoas tendon and the anterior hip joint capsule during hip flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

In roughly 15% of individuals it communicates directly with the hip joint cavity, so it can distend in the presence of a hip joint effusion; iliopsoas bursitis is a recognized cause of anterior groin pain and a palpable groin mass.

Subtendinous bursa of iliacus muscle.r.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of iliacus muscle
Subtendinous bursa of iliacus muscle.r.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF ILIACUS MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of the iliacus muscle lies between the iliacus tendon (as it joins the psoas major to form the iliopsoas) and the underlying iliac bone or hip joint capsule, closely related to the larger iliopectineal bursa.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the iliacus tendon and adjacent bone as the combined iliopsoas tendon glides during hip flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is functionally and anatomically related to iliopsoas bursitis and anterior hip impingement syndromes.

Superior bursa of biceps femoris muscle..description:
SUPERIOR BURSA OF BICEPS FEMORIS MUSCLE

The superior bursa of the biceps femoris muscle is a synovial sac located near the proximal (ischial) attachment of the long head of biceps femoris, close to the ischial tuberosity.

== Function ==

It reduces friction at the proximal hamstring origin as the muscle glides against adjacent structures during hip extension and knee flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

It may become symptomatic in proximal hamstring tendinopathy, a common overuse injury in runners and sprinters.

Subtendinous prepatellar bursa.r.description:
SUBTENDINOUS PREPATELLAR BURSA

The subtendinous prepatellar bursa is one of the layered prepatellar bursae, located between the quadriceps (patellar) tendon fibres and the anterior surface of the patella itself, deep to the subcutaneous and subfascial prepatellar bursae.

== Function ==

It allows the terminal fibres of the quadriceps tendon to glide smoothly over the anterior patella during knee flexion and extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is the deepest of the three prepatellar bursae and is less commonly affected by kneeling-related bursitis than the more superficial subcutaneous prepatellar bursa.

== Function ==

It allows the terminal fibres of the quadriceps tendon to glide smoothly over the anterior patella during knee flexion and extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is the deepest of the three prepatellar bursae and is less commonly affected by kneeling-related bursitis than the more superficial subcutaneous prepatellar bursa.

Subcutaneous prepatellar bursa.r.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS PREPATELLAR BURSA

The subcutaneous prepatellar bursa is a superficial synovial bursa located between the skin and the anterior surface of the patella.

== Function ==

It protects the front of the knee and allows the skin to glide freely over the patella during kneeling and knee flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is the bursa classically inflamed in prepatellar bursitis, also known as 'housemaid's knee,' a condition common among people who kneel frequently, such as carpet layers, roofers, and gardeners.

Subcutaneous prepatellar bursa.l.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS PREPATELLAR BURSA

The subcutaneous prepatellar bursa is a superficial synovial bursa located between the skin and the anterior surface of the patella.

== Function ==

It protects the front of the knee and allows the skin to glide freely over the patella during kneeling and knee flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

Deep infrapatellar bursa.r.description:
DEEP INFRAPATELLAR BURSA

The deep infrapatellar bursa lies between the posterior surface of the patellar ligament and the anterior surface of the proximal tibia, just above the tibial tuberosity.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the patellar tendon and the underlying tibia during knee flexion and extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

Deep infrapatellar bursitis is often related to repetitive jumping activities ('jumper's knee' spectrum) and, unlike the subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa, is not caused by direct kneeling trauma.

Deep infrapatellar bursa.l.description:
DEEP INFRAPATELLAR BURSA

The deep infrapatellar bursa lies between the posterior surface of the patellar ligament and the anterior surface of the proximal tibia, just above the tibial tuberosity.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the patellar tendon and the underlying tibia during knee flexion and extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

Deep infrapatellar bursitis is often related to repetitive jumping activities ('jumper's knee' spectrum) and, unlike the subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa, is not caused by direct kneeling trauma.

Medial patellar retinaculum.l.description:
MEDIAL PATELLAR RETINACULUM


The medial patellar retinaculum is the branch of the tendon of insertion of the quadriceps femoris that crosses the knee on the medial side of the patella. 

Most of the fibers of the medial patellar retinaculum originate in the medial femoral region from the vastus medialis muscle, just superior to the patella.

Subfacial prepatellar bursa.r.description:
SUBFASCIAL PREPATELLAR BURSA

The subfascial prepatellar bursa is the intermediate of the three prepatellar bursae, located between the deep fascia (fascia lata) overlying the knee and the quadriceps tendon anterior to the patella, situated between the more superficial subcutaneous prepatellar bursa and the deeper subtendinous prepatellar bursa.

== Function ==

It allows the deep fascia to glide over the quadriceps tendon and patella during knee movement.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is the least commonly affected of the three layered prepatellar bursae in clinical bursitis.

Subfacial prepatellar bursa.l.description:
SUBFASCIAL PREPATELLAR BURSA

The subfascial prepatellar bursa is the intermediate of the three prepatellar bursae, located between the deep fascia (fascia lata) overlying the knee and the quadriceps tendon anterior to the patella, situated between the more superficial subcutaneous prepatellar bursa and the deeper subtendinous prepatellar bursa.

Subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa.r.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS INFRAPATELLAR BURSA

The subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa (superficial infrapatellar bursa) lies between the skin and the anterior surface of the distal patellar ligament and tibial tuberosity.

== Function ==

It cushions the skin overlying the patellar tendon and tibial tuberosity, allowing the skin to glide during kneeling and knee flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

This bursa is prone to inflammation from direct kneeling pressure, producing swelling just below the kneecap, and must be distinguished clinically from the deep infrapatellar bursa.

Subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa.l.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS INFRAPATELLAR BURSA

Suprapatellar bursa.r.description:
SUPRAPATELLAR BURSA

The suprapatellar bursa (suprapatellar pouch or recess) lies between the quadriceps femoris tendon and the anterior surface of the distal femur, just proximal to the patella.

== Function ==

It acts as an extension of the knee joint's synovial cavity, with which it communicates in the large majority of adults, serving as an expansion chamber for synovial fluid during knee flexion and extension and allowing the quadriceps tendon to glide smoothly over the femur.

== Clinical relevance ==

Because it communicates freely with the knee joint, distension of the suprapatellar bursa (suprapatellar effusion) is a reliable clinical and imaging sign of intra-articular knee pathology, such as synovitis, hemarthrosis, or infection.

Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibi.displayName: Right Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibia
Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibi.baseName: Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibia
Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibi.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS BURSA OF TUBEROSITY OF TIBIA

The subcutaneous bursa of the tuberosity of the tibia is a small synovial sac located between the skin and the tibial tuberosity, distal to the patellar ligament insertion.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the skin and the bony tibial tuberosity during kneeling and direct pressure over the upper shin.

== Clinical relevance ==

It may become inflamed with repeated kneeling or direct trauma and should be distinguished from Osgood-Schlatter disease, which involves the tibial tuberosity apophysis itself rather than this bursa.

Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps fe.displayName: Right Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps femoris muscle
Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps fe.baseName: Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps femoris muscle
Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps fe.description:
INFERIOR SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF BICEPS FEMORIS MUSCLE

The inferior subtendinous bursa of the biceps femoris muscle is located between the distal biceps femoris tendon and the fibular collateral ligament of the knee, near the tendon's insertion on the head of the fibula.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the biceps femoris tendon and the adjacent fibular collateral ligament during knee flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is one of the lateral knee bursae that can be a source of posterolateral knee pain, sometimes confused with lateral meniscal or ligamentous injury.

Subtendinous bursa of sartorius muscle.r.displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of sartorius muscle
Subtendinous bursa of sartorius muscle.r.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF SARTORIUS MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of the sartorius muscle lies deep to the distal sartorius tendon at its insertion on the medial proximal tibia, as part of the pes anserinus tendon group along with gracilis and semitendinosus.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the sartorius tendon and the underlying tibial collateral ligament and bone.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is closely related to, and sometimes considered part of, the anserine bursa, and can be involved in pes anserine bursitis, a common cause of medial knee pain in runners.

Subtendinous bursa of sartorius muscle.l.description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF SARTORIUS MUSCLE

The subtendinous bursa of the sartorius muscle lies deep to the distal sartorius tendon at its insertion on the medial proximal tibia, as part of the pes anserinus tendon group along with gracilis and semitendinosus.

Anserine bursa.r.description:
ANSERINE BURSA


The anserine bursa (tibial intertendinous bursa) is a sub muscular bursa located deep to the pes anserinus on the anteromedial proximal tibia. 

Pes anserine bursitis is a common inflammatory condition of the anserine bursa.

Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemi.baseName: Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle
Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemi.description:
MEDIAL SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF GASTROCNEMIUS MUSCLE

The medial subtendinous bursa of the gastrocnemius muscle lies deep to the proximal tendon of origin of the medial head of gastrocnemius, between the tendon and the posteromedial femoral condyle, at the posterior aspect of the knee.

== Function ==

It allows the gastrocnemius tendon to glide over the femoral condyle during knee flexion and extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

This bursa frequently communicates with the semimembranosus bursa and the knee joint cavity; its distension is the classic anatomical basis of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst.

Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnem.displayName: Right Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle
Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnem.baseName: Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle
Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnem.description:
LATERAL SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF GASTROCNEMIUS MUSCLE

The lateral subtendinous bursa of the gastrocnemius muscle lies deep to the proximal tendon of origin of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, between the tendon and the posterolateral femoral condyle.

== Function ==

It reduces friction as the lateral gastrocnemius tendon glides over the lateral femoral condyle during knee movement.

== Clinical relevance ==

It may occasionally communicate with the popliteal recess of the knee joint and can contribute to posterolateral knee swelling.

Semimembranosus bursa.r.description:
SEMIMEMBRANOSUS BURSA

The semimembranosus bursa is located at the posteromedial aspect of the knee, between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle (or the medial tibial condyle, depending on the specific bursal component described).

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the semimembranosus tendon and adjacent structures during knee flexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

This bursa commonly communicates with the knee joint and with the medial gastrocnemius bursa; its distension is the most frequent anatomical origin of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst, which presents as posterior knee swelling.

The semimembranosus bursa is located at the posteromedial aspect of the knee, between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle (or the medial tibial condyle, depending on the specific bursal component described).

Subcutaneous bursa of lateral malleolus..displayName: Right Subcutaneous bursa of lateral malleolus
Subcutaneous bursa of lateral malleolus..description:
SUBCUTANEOUS BURSA OF LATERAL MALLEOLUS

The subcutaneous bursa of the lateral malleolus is a small synovial sac located between the skin and the bony prominence of the lateral malleolus (distal fibula).

== Function ==

It cushions and reduces friction between the skin and the lateral malleolus during ankle movement and against footwear or external pressure.

== Clinical relevance ==

It may become inflamed (lateral premalleolar bursitis) from ill-fitting footwear or repetitive friction, presenting as tender swelling over the outer ankle.

Subcutaneous bursa of medial malleolus.r.displayName: Right Subcutaneous bursa of medial malleolus
Subcutaneous bursa of medial malleolus.r.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS BURSA OF MEDIAL MALLEOLUS

The subcutaneous bursa of the medial malleolus is a small synovial sac located between the skin and the bony prominence of the medial malleolus (distal tibia).

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the skin and the medial malleolus during ankle movement, particularly under pressure from footwear or repetitive contact.

== Clinical relevance ==

Inflammation of this bursa (medial malleolar bursitis) can result from direct trauma, footwear friction, or a fall onto the ankle, producing localized swelling and tenderness.

Subtendinous bursa of tibialis anterior..displayName: Right Subtendinous bursa of tibialis anterior
Subtendinous bursa of tibialis anterior..description:
SUBTENDINOUS BURSA OF TIBIALIS ANTERIOR

The subtendinous bursa of tibialis anterior is a small synovial sac located deep to the distal tendon of the tibialis anterior muscle, near its insertion on the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal bone.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the tibialis anterior tendon and the underlying bone or ligament at its insertion during ankle dorsiflexion and inversion.

== Clinical relevance ==

It is distinct from the tendon's synovial sheath and can occasionally be a source of localized dorsomedial midfoot pain.

Subcutaneous calcaneal bursa.r.description:
SUBCUTANEOUS CALCANEAL BURSA

The subcutaneous calcaneal bursa (also called the retroachilleal or Achilles bursa) lies between the skin and the posterior aspect of the distal calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, just above its insertion on the calcaneus.

== Function ==

It protects the calcaneal tendon and skin from external pressure, such as from the heel counter of a shoe.

== Clinical relevance ==

Inflammation of this superficial bursa, often related to footwear friction, produces a tender lump behind the heel and is a common component of insertional Achilles tendon pathology alongside Haglund's deformity.

Subtendinous calcaneal bursa.r.description:
SUBTENDINOUS CALCANEAL BURSA

The subtendinous calcaneal bursa (retrocalcaneal bursa) is located between the anterior surface of the distal calcaneal (Achilles) tendon and the posterosuperior surface of the calcaneus, anterior to Kager's fat pad.

== Function ==

It reduces friction between the calcaneal tendon and the calcaneus during ankle plantarflexion and dorsiflexion.

== Clinical relevance ==

Retrocalcaneal bursitis is a common cause of posterior heel pain and is frequently associated with Haglund's deformity (a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal process) and insertional Achilles tendinopathy.

Intertubercular tendon sheath.r.description:
INTERTUBERCULAR TENDON SHEATH

The intertubercular tendon sheath is a synovial sheath that envelops the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii as it passes through the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus, between the greater and lesser tubercles. It is a direct extension of the glenohumeral joint capsule and communicates with it proximally.

== Function ==

It reduces friction and permits smooth gliding of the biceps tendon within the bony groove during shoulder movement, while the transverse humeral ligament and rotator interval structures help stabilize the tendon within it.

== Clinical relevance ==

Because it communicates with the joint capsule, fluid within this sheath (biceps tenosynovitis) often reflects underlying glenohumeral joint or rotator cuff pathology; it is also a common site of biceps tendon instability and rupture.

Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus..displayName: Right Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus..baseName: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus..description:
TENDON SHEATH OF FLEXOR POLLICIS LONGUS

The tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus (radial bursa) is a synovial sheath that encloses the flexor pollicis longus tendon from just proximal to the carpal tunnel to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb, lying on the radial side of the carpal tunnel.

== Function ==

It reduces friction and allows the flexor pollicis longus tendon to glide smoothly beneath the flexor retinaculum and along the thumb during flexion of the interphalangeal joint.

== Clinical relevance ==

The radial bursa may communicate with the common flexor tendon sheath (ulnar bursa) in a minority of individuals, which has implications for the spread of infection ('horseshoe abscess') in flexor tendon sheath infections of the hand.

Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis.r.description:
TENDON SHEATH OF FLEXOR CARPI RADIALIS

The tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis is a synovial sheath enclosing the flexor carpi radialis tendon within its own separate fibro-osseous tunnel, formed by a reflection of the flexor retinaculum, at the radial margin of the carpal tunnel.

== Function ==

It reduces friction as the tendon passes along the volar aspect of the scaphoid and trapezium en route to its insertion on the base of the second metacarpal.

== Clinical relevance ==

Tenosynovitis of this sheath can cause radial-sided wrist pain and swelling and lies close to the scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal joint, with which symptoms can overlap.

Common flexor tendon sheath.r.description:
COMMON FLEXOR TENDON SHEATH

The common flexor tendon sheath (ulnar bursa) is a large synovial sheath that encloses the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus, beginning proximal to the wrist crease, passing through the carpal tunnel, and extending into the palm; it typically remains continuous with the synovial sheath of the little finger.

== Function ==

It allows the long flexor tendons of the fingers to glide together with minimal friction beneath the flexor retinaculum and through the carpal tunnel.

== Clinical relevance ==

Thickening or inflammation of the synovium within this sheath is a major contributor to carpal tunnel syndrome, and infection here can spread proximally into the forearm.

== Function ==

It allows the long flexor tendons of the fingers to glide together with minimal friction beneath the flexor retinaculum and through the carpal tunnel.

== Clinical relevance ==

Thickening or inflammation of the synovium within this sheath is a major contributor to carpal tunnel syndrome, and infection here can spread proximally into the forearm.

Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris..displayName: Left Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris..baseName: Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris..description:
TENDON SHEATH OF EXTENSOR CARPI ULNARIS

The tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris is a synovial sheath enclosing the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon within the sixth dorsal compartment of the wrist, in a groove near the base of the ulnar styloid process, deep to the extensor retinaculum.

== Function ==

It reduces friction as the tendon glides within its osseofibrous tunnel during wrist extension and ulnar deviation.

== Clinical relevance ==

Instability or subluxation of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon out of this sheath, and tenosynovitis within it, are recognized causes of ulnar-sided wrist pain, particularly in racquet-sport athletes.

Synovial sheaths of digits of hand.r.displayName: Right Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Synovial sheaths of digits of hand.r.baseName: Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Synovial sheaths of digits of hand.r.description:
SYNOVIAL SHEATHS OF DIGITS OF HAND

The synovial sheaths of the digits of the hand are tubular synovial linings that surround the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons (and flexor pollicis longus in the thumb) as they pass through the fibrous digital sheaths of each finger, from the level of the metacarpal head to the distal phalanx.

== Function ==

They provide a lubricated, low-friction surface that allows the flexor tendons to glide freely within the fibro-osseous digital tunnels during finger flexion, while a mesotendon (vincula) carries blood supply to the tendon.

== Clinical relevance ==

Infection or inflammation of these sheaths (flexor tenosynovitis, or 'trigger finger' when associated with the A1 pulley) can cause pain, swelling, and restricted digital movement, and pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency due to the risk of tendon necrosis.

Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digi.displayName: Right Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digit of hand
Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digi.baseName: Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digit of hand
Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digi.description:
CRUCIFORM PART OF FIBROUS SHEATH OF DIGIT OF HAND

The cruciform part of the fibrous sheath of the digit of the hand consists of three thin, cross-shaped (X-shaped) fibrous bands, known as the cruciate pulleys (C1-C3), located between the thicker annular pulleys (A1-A5) along the palmar surface of each finger: C1 lies between A2 and A3, C2 between A3 and A4, and C3 between A4 and A5.

== Function ==

Unlike the annular pulleys, the cruciate pulleys are thin and flexible, allowing the fibrous digital sheath to fold and collapse during finger flexion without restricting movement, while still helping to maintain alignment of the flexor tendons and prevent bowstringing.

== Clinical relevance ==

Because they are thinner and more flexible than the annular pulleys, the cruciate pulleys are less commonly implicated in trigger finger, which classically involves the A1 annular pulley.

Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi.displayName: Right Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus
Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi.baseName: Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus
Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi.description:
TENDON SHEATH OF EXTENSOR DIGITI MINIMI MANUS

The tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus is a synovial sheath enclosing the extensor digiti minimi tendon within the fifth dorsal compartment of the wrist, positioned over the distal radioulnar joint, deep to the extensor retinaculum.

== Function ==

It allows the extensor digiti minimi tendon to glide smoothly as it extends the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint.

== Clinical relevance ==

Tenosynovitis of the fifth compartment can occur in inflammatory arthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis and may predispose to extensor tendon rupture at the wrist.

Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longu.displayName: Right Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longu.baseName: Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longu.description:
TENDON SHEATH OF EXTENSOR POLLICIS LONGUS

The tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus is a synovial sheath enclosing the extensor pollicis longus tendon within the third dorsal compartment of the wrist, where the tendon angles sharply around the bony prominence of Lister's tubercle on the distal radius before crossing obliquely to the thumb.

== Function ==

It reduces friction as the tendon changes direction around Lister's tubercle, which acts as a pulley during thumb extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

The sharp angulation around Lister's tubercle makes this tendon and its sheath prone to attritional rupture, notably as a delayed complication of distal radius fractures.

Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - e.displayName: Right Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - ext. pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - e.baseName: Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - ext. pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - e.description:
TENDON SHEATH OF ABDUCTOR POLLICIS LONGUS AND EXTENSOR POLLICIS BREVIS

This tendon sheath is a shared synovial sheath enclosing the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis within the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, at the radial aspect of the distal radius; these tendons form the radial border of the anatomical snuffbox.

== Function ==

It allows both tendons to glide together with minimal friction during thumb abduction and extension.

== Clinical relevance ==

Inflammation of this sheath produces De Quervain's tenosynovitis, a common overuse condition causing pain over the radial styloid, classically elicited by the Finkelstein test.

Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radiali.displayName: Right Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis
Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radiali.baseName: Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis
Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radiali.description:
TENDON SHEATH OF EXTENSORS CARPI RADIALIS

The tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis encloses the tendons of extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis in separate synovial compartments within the second dorsal compartment of the wrist, lying along the posterior surface of the radius, between the first and third dorsal compartments.

== Function ==

It reduces friction and allows both radial wrist extensor tendons to glide smoothly during wrist extension and radial deviation.

== Clinical relevance ==

Second-compartment tenosynovitis, sometimes called 'intersection syndrome' when it involves the crossing point with the first compartment tendons, presents with pain and swelling on the dorsoradial forearm proximal to the wrist.
